body:
Source of atmospheric energy

The Sun supplies almost all the energy responsible for the Earth's weather and climate. Solar energy drives evaporation, atmospheric circulation and many oceanic processes.

Insolation is incoming solar radiation received by the Earth. Incoming solar radiation is a mnemonic for the term.

Solar radiation travels through space as electromagnetic radiation. Because the Sun is much hotter than the Earth's surface, it emits most of its energy at relatively short wavelengths, including visible light, ultraviolet radiation and near-infrared radiation.

Angle of incidence of solar rays

The amount of solar energy received per unit area depends greatly on the angle at which sunlight strikes a surface.

Nearly vertical rays concentrate their energy over a smaller surface area. Oblique or slanting rays distribute the same amount of energy over a larger surface area, reducing the energy received per unit area.

Slanting rays also travel through a greater thickness of the atmosphere before reaching the surface. This increases the opportunity for atmospheric scattering and absorption.

Factors controlling surface insolation

FactorEffect
LatitudeControls the typical angle of incoming solar rays.
Earth's rotationProduces day and night and changes the solar angle during the day.
Length of daylightDetermines the duration of solar-energy receipt.
Earth's axial tilt and revolutionProduce seasonal variations in solar angle and day length.
Atmospheric transparencyClouds, gases and aerosols affect the passage of sunlight.
Slope and aspectDetermine how directly sunlight strikes an inclined surface.
Earth–Sun distanceProduces a smaller annual variation in incoming solar energy.

Earth–Sun distance

The Earth revolves around the Sun in a slightly elliptical orbit. Consequently, the distance between the Earth and the Sun changes during the year.

  • Perihelion: The Earth is nearest to the Sun, usually in early January, at a distance of approximately 147 million km.
  • Aphelion: The Earth is farthest from the Sun, usually in early July, at a distance of approximately 152 million km.

The dates are approximately 3 January and 4 July in conventional textbook descriptions, but the exact dates vary from year to year.

Other conditions being equal, the Earth receives a greater intensity of solar radiation at perihelion than at aphelion. However, this variation is not the principal cause of seasons. The Northern Hemisphere experiences winter around perihelion because it is tilted away from the Sun during that part of its orbit.

Direct and diffuse solar radiation

Some solar radiation reaches the surface directly from the Sun. This is called direct radiation. Radiation scattered by atmospheric molecules, aerosols and clouds that subsequently reaches the surface is called diffuse radiation.

Both contribute to surface insolation. Therefore, a cloudy day may receive significant solar energy even when the Sun is not directly visible.

A pyranometer measures solar irradiance received over a hemisphere; when horizontally exposed, it measures both direct and diffuse solar radiation reaching a horizontal surface. Irradiance is commonly expressed in watts per square metre (W/m2).

Prelims focus

  • Insolation is incoming solar radiation.
  • Vertical rays concentrate energy over a smaller area than oblique rays.
  • Perihelion occurs in early January; aphelion occurs in early July.
  • Diffuse radiation can reach the Earth's surface after atmospheric scattering.
  • A pyranometer measures solar irradiance.
  • Trap: The variation in Earth–Sun distance is not the main cause of seasons.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Solar Radiation and Variability of Insolation at the Surface of the Earth, pp. 67–68; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 9, Temperature, pp. 62–63, 66.]

pictures.caption: Solar angle and energy received per unit area.

title: Insolation: Incoming Solar Radiation and Its Controls

body:
Why insolation varies with latitude

The spherical shape of the Earth causes solar rays to strike different latitudes at different angles. Low latitudes generally receive more concentrated solar radiation, whereas high latitudes receive increasingly oblique rays.

Consequently, average annual insolation generally decreases from low latitudes towards the poles. The distribution is modified by atmospheric transparency, cloud cover, surface orientation and seasonal changes in daylight duration.

Earth's axial inclination and seasons

The Earth's rotational axis is inclined by approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane. Equivalently, the axis makes an angle of approximately 66.5° with the orbital plane itself.

As the Earth revolves around the Sun, the direction of its axial tilt remains approximately constant. Different hemispheres therefore become inclined towards the Sun during different parts of the year.

A hemisphere tilted towards the Sun experiences a higher solar angle and longer daylight duration. These conditions increase solar-energy receipt and produce summer. The opposite hemisphere receives less solar energy and experiences winter.

Solstices and equinoxes

Approximate dateOverhead midday SunNorthern Hemisphere
21 MarchEquatorSpring equinox
21 JuneTropic of Cancer, 23.5° NSummer solstice
23 SeptemberEquatorAutumn equinox
22 DecemberTropic of Capricorn, 23.5° SWinter solstice

These conventional dates are approximate. Exact astronomical dates can vary slightly between years.

During an equinox, day and night are approximately equal in duration across the Earth. During the June solstice, daylight is longest in most of the Northern Hemisphere and shortest in most of the Southern Hemisphere. The situation reverses during the December solstice.

Heat zones of the Earth

  • Torrid zone: Extends between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. The midday Sun can be directly overhead at least once a year.
  • Temperate zones: Extend between the tropics and the corresponding polar circles, approximately 23.5° to 66.5° latitude in each hemisphere.
  • Frigid zones: Extend from the Arctic and Antarctic Circles to their respective poles, approximately 66.5° to 90° latitude.

Outside the tropics, the midday Sun never reaches the zenith, the point directly overhead.

The polar circles mark the approximate latitudinal limits beyond which continuous daylight or continuous darkness can occur for at least one full day. At the poles, these periods extend to approximately 6 months each.

Gujarat connection

The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat. Places located south of this latitude within the state can experience the Sun directly overhead on appropriate dates. Places north of the Tropic of Cancer cannot experience an overhead Sun.

Why maximum surface insolation is not always at the equator

Equatorial regions receive relatively direct sunlight throughout the year, but frequent cloud cover and atmospheric moisture reduce the amount of solar radiation reaching the ground.

Subtropical deserts commonly experience clearer skies and greater atmospheric transparency. They can therefore receive more average surface insolation than cloudy equatorial regions.

Similarly, high-latitude regions can receive substantial total daily solar radiation during summer because daylight lasts for a long time. This does not alter the general decline in annual insolation towards the poles.

Distinguish the angle of solar rays, the duration of daylight and the actual energy reaching the surface. They influence insolation together, and no single factor determines every geographical pattern.

Prelims focus

  • Earth's axial tilt is approximately 23.5° from the perpendicular to its orbital plane.
  • The overhead Sun migrates between 23.5° N and 23.5° S.
  • June solstice: overhead Sun at the Tropic of Cancer.
  • December solstice: overhead Sun at the Tropic of Capricorn.
  • Clear subtropical deserts can receive greater surface insolation than cloudy equatorial regions.
  • Trap: The equator does not necessarily receive the maximum surface insolation.

[References: NCERT, Class 6, The Earth: Our Habitat, 2018–19, Chapters 2 and 3, Heat Zones of the Earth and Motions of the Earth, pp. 11–12, 18–21; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Spatial Distribution of Insolation, p. 68.]

pictures.caption: Annual variation in the position of the overhead Sun.

title: Latitudinal and Seasonal Distribution of Insolation

body:
Solar radiation and terrestrial radiation

Solar energy reaching the Earth is partly reflected, partly absorbed by the atmosphere and partly absorbed by the Earth's surface.

Much of the incoming visible and shortwave radiation passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by land and water. The warmed surface then emits energy at longer infrared wavelengths. This outgoing energy emitted by the Earth's surface is called terrestrial radiation.

FeatureSolar radiationTerrestrial radiation
Principal sourceSunEarth's surface
Typical wavelengthRelatively shortRelatively long infrared
Occurrence at a placeDuring daylightDuring day and night
Major roleSupplies energyTransfers thermal energy from the surface

The atmosphere absorbs some incoming solar radiation directly. Nevertheless, heating from the Earth's surface is a major source of energy for the lower troposphere.

Conduction

Conduction is the transfer of heat through direct molecular contact, without bulk movement of the material.

During the day, a sun-heated land surface can transfer heat to the air immediately touching it. At night, a rapidly cooling surface can instead receive heat from the adjacent air, thereby cooling that air.

Because air is a relatively poor conductor of heat, conduction is especially important within the thin layer of air directly in contact with the Earth's surface.

Convection

Convection involves heat transfer through the movement of a fluid, particularly the vertical movement of air in meteorology.

Air heated near the ground expands and can become less dense than the surrounding air. It then rises through buoyancy. Cooler air moves towards the surface to replace it, creating circulation.

Rising air encounters lower atmospheric pressure, expands and cools. If sufficiently moist, it may reach saturation and form clouds.

Advection

Advection is the horizontal transport of atmospheric properties, such as heat and moisture, by moving air.

Warm winds can raise temperatures in the regions into which they blow, while cold winds can lower them. The hot, dry summer wind known as the loo in northern and northwestern India is an example of warm-air advection.

Latent heat transfer

When liquid water evaporates, it absorbs energy from its surroundings. This energy is carried in the resulting water vapour. When the vapour subsequently condenses, latent heat is released into the atmosphere.

Evaporation therefore cools the evaporating surface, while condensation provides energy to the surrounding atmosphere. This process is particularly important in moist tropical regions and cloud development.

Heating and cooling through radiation

Unlike conduction, radiation does not require direct molecular contact. It can travel through a vacuum. The Earth receives solar radiation through space and continuously loses thermal energy through infrared radiation.

During the day, incoming solar energy often exceeds the surface's energy losses, causing warming. At night, the absence of insolation allows continuing energy losses to cool the surface.

Prelims focus

  • Solar radiation is predominantly shortwave; terrestrial radiation is predominantly longwave.
  • Conduction transfers heat through direct molecular contact.
  • Convection involves vertical air movement in atmospheric heating.
  • Advection transports heat horizontally.
  • Evaporation absorbs latent heat; condensation releases it.
  • Trap: The Earth's surface emits terrestrial radiation during both day and night.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Heating and Cooling of Atmosphere and Terrestrial Radiation, pp. 68–69; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, reprint 2020, Chapter 9, Temperature, pp. 62–65; NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget, 2009, consulted 28 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Conduction heats air touching warm ground; convection lifts warmer air as cooler air replaces it; advection carries warm or cold air horizontally.
pictures.caption: Three mechanisms of atmospheric heat transfer.

pictures.alt: Evaporation absorbs latent heat and cools the surface; water vapour carries energy upward, and condensation releases it to the atmosphere.
pictures.caption: Latent heat absorption and release.

title: Heating and Cooling of the Atmosphere

body:
Natural regulation of surface temperature

Earth's atmosphere allows a substantial proportion of incoming solar radiation to reach the surface. Land and water absorb this energy, become warmer and emit infrared radiation.

Some of the emitted infrared radiation escapes directly to space. Atmospheric gases and clouds absorb part of the remaining radiation and emit infrared energy in different directions, including back towards the surface.

The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere resulting from the absorption and emission of infrared radiation by greenhouse gases and clouds.

The greenhouse effect does not prevent heat from escaping permanently. Instead, greenhouse gases alter the way energy is transferred through the atmosphere and emitted into space. A warmer surface can eventually emit more radiation, helping restore energy balance.

Important greenhouse gases

GasMajor atmospheric significance
Water vapour (H2O)Major contributor to the natural greenhouse effect
Carbon dioxide (CO2)Important long-lived greenhouse gas
Methane (CH4)Absorbs infrared radiation
Nitrous oxide (N2O)Long-lived greenhouse gas
Ozone (O3)Absorbs infrared and ultraviolet radiation
Halogenated greenhouse gasesInclude several human-produced gases that absorb infrared radiation

Nitrogen and oxygen together form approximately 99% of dry atmospheric air, but they are not significant greenhouse gases under ordinary atmospheric conditions.

The effectiveness of a greenhouse gas depends on its ability to absorb infrared radiation, its concentration and its atmospheric behaviour, not simply on its abundance.

Natural and enhanced greenhouse effects

The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth's surface substantially warmer than it would otherwise be. It is an essential part of the climate system and supports conditions suitable for life.

Increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases strengthen the greenhouse effect. Human activities such as fossil-fuel combustion and certain land-use changes increase atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations. The resulting additional warming is associated with the enhanced greenhouse effect.

Water vapour responds strongly to temperature. Warmer conditions generally allow more water vapour to remain in the atmosphere where moisture is available. The additional water vapour can further strengthen the greenhouse effect, creating a positive feedback.

Clouds and surface temperature

Clouds influence both incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation.

  • During the day, clouds reflect part of the incoming sunlight and may reduce surface heating.
  • During the night, clouds absorb and emit infrared radiation, often reducing the rate of surface cooling.

Consequently, cloudy days often experience lower daytime maximum temperatures and cloudy nights often experience higher minimum temperatures than otherwise comparable clear conditions. Cloudy conditions therefore commonly reduce the daily temperature range.

Ozone depletion and the greenhouse effect are different processes. Ozone depletion concerns reduced protection from solar ultraviolet radiation. The greenhouse effect principally concerns absorption and emission of terrestrial infrared radiation.

Prelims focus

  • Greenhouse gases absorb and emit terrestrial infrared radiation.
  • The natural greenhouse effect is essential for maintaining a habitable climate.
  • Water vapour is an important natural greenhouse gas.
  • Cloud cover often reduces daytime heating and nighttime cooling.
  • Nitrogen and oxygen are not significant greenhouse gases.
  • Trap: The greenhouse effect does not operate primarily by blocking incoming visible sunlight.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018–19, Chapter 4, Air, pp. 20–21; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, reprint 2025–26, Chapter 7, p. 64, and reprint 2026–27, Chapter 8, Terrestrial Radiation, pp. 68–69; NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget, 2009; UNEP Ozone Secretariat, 20 Questions and Answers, 2022 assessment, online sources consulted 28 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Radiative processes responsible for the greenhouse effect.

title: The Greenhouse Effect and Earth's Thermal Regulation
